::: center
**Handout 27\
Null Hypothesis Tests for Means**
:::

::: exer
**Exercise 1**. Did the New England Patriots deliberately deflate
footballs in an NFL playoff game against the Indianapolis Colts on
January 18, 2015? The following table[^1] summarizes the decrease in air
pressure (psi), from pre-game to halftime, for the footballs from each
team that were checked at halftime by officials.
:::

  Team         Observed values of decrease in air pressure (psi)                                                                         Size    Mean      SD
  ---------- --------------------------------------------------- ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------- -------
  Patriots                                                  1.00   1.65   1.35   1.80   1.40   0.90   0.65   1.40   1.55   2.00   1.60     11   1.391   0.402
  Colts                                                     0.30   0.25   0.50   0.45                                                       4   0.375   0.119

1.  Compute the observed difference in sample means.

    **Solution:** $\bar{x}_{P} - \bar{x}_C = 1.391 - 0.375 = 1.016$ psi\

2.  Suppose we want to assess if it is plausible that the Patriots
    didn't interfere with the footballs, and the observed difference in
    means is just due to chance. What would we assume in order to run
    our simulation? (For example, what we would assume about the two
    footballs in the first column with observed values of 1.00 and
    0.30?)

    **Solution:** If there is no difference, assume value of the psi
    decrease (response variable) would be the same regardless of team
    (explanatory variable group)\

3.  Specify how the "null distribution" of the statistic could be
    simulated with cards.

    -   We can use 15 cards cards.

    -   On each card we would write an observed value of decrease in psi
        (response), e.g., 1.00, 0.30m 1.65, 0.25, etc

    -   Shuffle the cards and deal 11 to represent Pats.

    -   The remaining 4 cards represent Colts.

    -   After shuffling and dealing, compute the mean for Pats, the mean
        for Colts, and the hypothetical difference in means
        $\bar{x}_P-\bar{x}_C$.

    -   Then repeat many times, each time recording the hypothetical
        difference in means $\bar{x}_P-\bar{x}_C$.

    -   To estimate the p-value: find the proportion of repetitions for
        which the difference in means was as extreme as the observed
        value 1.016\

4.  Use cards to perform one repetition of the above simulation, record
    the results here, and compute the appropriate difference in means.

    ::: center
      Team         *Shuffled* values of decrease in air pressure (psi)                                                                                             Size     Mean
      ---------- ----------------------------------------------------- -------- -------- -------- -------- -------- -------- -------- -------- -------- -------- ------ --------
      Patriots                                                                                                                                                       11         
      Colts                                                                                          X        X        X        X        X        X        X          4 
    :::

5.  The following plot displays results from an applet used to run 10000
    repetitions of the simulation (the plot on the left is the results
    from just the first 100 repetitions). Estimate the probability of
    observing a difference in means as extreme as 1.016 just by chance.

    Enter observed difference in means, $\bar{x}_P-\bar{x}_C =1.016$
    into the "as extreme as" box and find the proportion of repetitions
    with a difference in means as extreme as 1.016

    <figure>
    <div class="minipage">
    <img src="C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/applet_patriots1"
    style="width:70.0%" />
    </div>
    <div class="minipage">
    <img src="C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/applet_patriots2"

6.  Is it plausible that the observed difference in means is just due to
    random chance?

    **Solution:** No. With a p-value $<0.0001$, we would not expect to
    see a difference as large as 1.016 just by random chance. If there
    were no difference in psi between the teams, we could only see a
    difference in means as large as 1.016 in fewer than 0.01% of
    samples. We have evidence that the Patriots footballs tended to
    deflate more than the Colts footballs.\

7.  Based on these data alone, do we have convincing evidence that the
    Patriots deliberately deflated the footballs? That is, were the
    Patriots the cause of the deflation?

    **Solution:** Not an experiment; the footballs were not randomly
    assigned to the teams. The teams brings their own footballs.
    Possible confounding variables. Maybe Pats just got bad quality
    footballs that tended to deflate more.\

-   Statisticians view conjectures about a population as two competing
    *hypotheses* about the population or process. These hypotheses
    usually constitute claims about the values of certain parameters.

-   A statistical **(null) hypothesis test** consists of using data to
    make a decision regarding these two explanations (hypotheses).

-   The **null hypothesis**, denoted $H_0$, represents the "status
    quo/no difference/no effect/no association" hypothesis.

    -   If the null hypothesis true then any observed
        difference/effect/association is just due to "random chance"
        resulting from natural sample-to-sample variability

-   The **alternative hypothesis**, denoted $H_a$ (or $H_1$), typically
    corresponds to what the researchers are hoping to gather evidence to
    support, and thus is a statement in line with the research
    conjecture

-   A statistical hypothesis test assesses if the data provide evidence
    to rule out the "random chance" explanation (which corresponds to
    the null hypothesis) in favor of the explanation provided by the
    research conjecture (alternative hypothesis).

-   The null hypothesis is often of the form
    $$H_0: \text{parameter} = \text{hypothesized value}$$ where the
    hypothesized value is a specific number determined by the research
    question (often 0 for "no difference").

-   The alternative hypotheses is often of one of the followinf forms
    $$\begin{aligned}
        \text{Case 1a:}\quad  H_a: \text{parameter} &> \text{hypothesized value}\\
        \text{Case 1b:}\quad H_a: \text{parameter} &< \text{hypothesized value}\\
        \text{Case 2:}\quad H_a: \text{parameter} &\neq \text{hypothesized value (``two-sided'')}
    \end{aligned}$$ Which of the three cases above is appropriate is
    determined by the research conjecture. When in doubt, use a
    two-sided ($\neq$) alternative.

-   Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are commonly used in
    conjunction

-   A confidence interval

    -   provides a range of plausible values

    -   but the cut-off between plausible and implausible is arbitrary
        (e.g. 95% confidence corresponds to $\alpha_0=0.05$)

        -   But be especially careful about interpreting confidence when
            conducting multiple confidence intervals.

-   A null hypothesis significance test

    -   Considers the plausibility of only a single hypothesized value

    -   But provides a precise measure --- the p-value --- of the
        plausibility of the particular hypothesized value in light of
        the observed data

        -   But be especially careful about interpreting p-values when
            conducting multiple hypothesis tests.

-   To assess the plausibility of the random chance explanation for the
    observed --- corresponding to the null hypothesis being true --- we
    need to know the pattern of sample-to-sample variability of the
    statistic that would be expected just due to random chance if the
    null hypothesis were true. This is called the **null distribution**
    of the statistic.

-   If the actual observed value of the statistic is not consistent with
    this pattern, then we have convincing evidence that the results did
    not occur by random chance alone, and we have evidence to reject the
    null hypothesis

-   The (simulated) null distribution provides a picture of what typical
    values of the statistic would be expected just by random chance
    alone if the null hypothesis were true.

-   The question is then: how surprising is the result we actually
    observed from the perspective of the null distribution? If the
    result would be very surprising, then "random chance" is not a
    plausible explanation for the observed result.

-   This gives us evidence to rule out a "random chance" explanation
    like in favor of a "research conjecture" explanation.

-   In other words, the more surprising the observed result would be
    just due to random chance, the stronger the evidence to **reject the
    null hypothesis** in favor of the alternative hypothesis.

-   We quantify "how surprising" with a p-value.

    -   The **p-value** is the probability of observing a value at least
        as extreme as the value actually observed, when the null
        hypothesis is true.

    -   The p-value can be estimated by the proportion (out of the total
        number of repetitions) of values in the simulated null
        distribution that are *at least as extreme* as the actual
        observed value of the statistic.

        -   Which tail(s) constitutes "at least as extreme\" is
            determined by the form of the *alternative hypothesis*

-   The smaller the p-value --- that is, the closer the p-value is to 0
    --- the less plausible it is that the observed result occurred just
    by random chance alone.

-   Thus, **the smaller the p-value the stronger the evidence to reject
    the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative hypothesis.**

-   If the observed results provide strong evidence that the data did
    not arise by random chance alone --- that is, when the p-value is
    small --- then there is evidence of a **statistical difference**.

-   How small is small enough? You should think of a sliding scale: the
    closer the p-value gets to 0 the stronger the evidence to reject the
    null hypothesis in favor of the alternative. Some guidelines, which
    should *not* be followed too strictly (especially when performing
    many hypothesis tests simultaneously):

    ::: center
      p-value                  Evidence to reject the null hypothesis?
      ------------------------ -----------------------------------------
      Above 0.10               Little to no evidence
      Between 0.01 and 0.10    Weak evidence
      Between 0.001 and 0.01   Moderate evidence
      Less than 0.001          Strong evidence
    :::

-   Do NOT rely strictly on arbitrary thresholds like p-value $<$ 0.05.\

::: {#exer:backpack .exer}
**Exercise 2**. Carrying a heavy backpack can be a source of "chronic,
low-level trauma," and can cause chronic shoulder, neck, and back pain.
The American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons recommends that a backpack
not weigh more than 10 percent of the wearer's body weight. Do Cal Poly
students follow this recommendation? That is, do the backpacks of Cal
Poly students weigh, on average, less than 10% of their bodyweight? The
JMP output summarizes data on a sample of 100 Cal Poly students.
:::

![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/backpack2){width="80%"}

1.  Identify the main parameter of interest with both words and an
    appropriate symbol.

    **Solution:** $\mu=$population mean backpack weight as percent of
    bodyweight for CP students.\

2.  Translate the research question into a hypothesis testing problem by
    specifying, with both words and appropriate symbols, the null
    hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis.

    **Solution:** The hypothesized value comes from the 10 percent
    recommendation.

    $H_0:\mu = 10$, population mean backpack weight as percent of body
    weight for CP students is 10 percent

    $H_a:\mu < 10$, population mean backpack weight as percent of body
    weight for CP students is less than 10 percent\

3.  Identify the null distribution of sample means. Then compute the
    p-value.

    **Solution:** The SE $s/\sqrt{n} = 3.66/\sqrt{100} = 0.366$ measures
    the sample-to-sample variability of sample mean backpack weight as
    percent of body weight for many hypothetical samples of 100 students
    each.

    $$\frac{\text{observed}-\text{hypothesized}}{\text{SE}}
    = \frac{7.71-10}{0.366} = \frac{-2.29}{0.366} = -6.3$$ The observed
    sample mean of 7.71 percent is 6.3 SEs below what we would expect if
    the null hypothesis were true. the p-value will be essentially 0.\

4.  Write a carefully worded sentence reporting your conclusion in
    context.

    **Solution:** With a p-value $<0.0001$, we have strong evidence to
    reject the null hypothesis and conclude population mean backpack
    weight as percent of bodyweight for CP students is less than 10
    percent.\

5.  Compute an appropriate 99% confidence interval.

    **Solution:** Observed $\pm$ multiple of SE. The multiple for 99%
    confidence is 2.6. $7.71 \pm 2.6\times 0.366$: $7.71 \pm 0.95$:
    $[6.7, 8.7]$\

6.  Write a sentence reporting your confidence interval in context.

    **Solution:** We estimate with 99% confidence that population mean
    backpack weight as percent of bodyweight for CP students is between
    6.7 and 8.7 percent. (The reason why "percent" here is because they
    are the measurement units of the variable.)\

7.  In generalizing your conclusions to Cal Poly students, what are you
    assuming?

    **Solution:** Reasonably representative random sample. Need to know
    more information about how the data were collected to investigate.\

8.  Do Cal Poly students follow the 10% recommendation? Is the analysis
    above the only way to address this question? Can you suggest
    another?

    **Solution:** The above just tells us that the *mean* is less than
    10%. But there might be individual students with backpacks that
    weigh more than 10% of their bodyweight. What proportion of students
    is this true for? For the sample, the 75th percentile is 9.6, so
    about 25% of students have backpacks that weigh more than 10 pecent
    of bodyweights. With $\hat{p}=0.25$, and SE of
    $\sqrt{0.25(1-0.25)}/\sqrt{100}=  0.043$, the 95% CI is
    $0.25 \pm 2 \times 0.043$: $[0.16, 0.34]$. We estimate with 95%
    confidence that the population proportion of CP students with
    backpacks that weigh more than 10 percent of their body weight is
    between 0.16 and 0.34. That is, we estimate with 95% confidence that
    between 16% and 34% of CP students have backpacks that weigh more
    than 10 percent of their bodyweights.\

-   **One-sample $t$ test**

-   Situation: question concerns a single numerical variable of interest

-   Parameter: $\mu$ is the population mean (i.e. the mean value of the
    variable over all units in the population)

-   Goal: assess the plausibility of a claim about $\mu$ regarding a
    hypothesized value $\mu_0$

-   The null hypothesis is $H_0: \mu= \mu_0$

-   The alternative hypothesis is one of $H_a: \mu >\mu_0$,
    $H_a: \mu<\mu_0$, or $H_a: \mu\neq \mu_0$

-   Statistics: $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean; $s$ is the sample standard
    deviation

-   Test statistic: the standardized value of $\bar{x}$, where

    -   the mean is computed assuming the null hypothesis,
        $H_0: \mu=\mu_0$, is true, and

    -   the unknown SD ($\sigma/\sqrt{n}$) is estimated with the
        standard error $s/\sqrt{n}$

    $$t = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}$$

-   The p-value is the probability of observing a value at least as
    extreme as $t$, in the tail direction indicated by the alternative
    hypothesis, for the $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
    (When in doubt, use a two-sided alternative and a two-tailed
    p-value.)

-   Assumptions:

    -   Simple random sample from a large population, that is,
        independent observations

    -   No bias in data collection

    -   Population mean is the parameter you want to estimate

::: exer
**Exercise 3**. Do newborns from mothers who smoke tend to weight less
at birth than newborns from mothers who don't smoke? The following
summarizes data on a sample of cases in North Carolina over a one year
period.
:::

![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/babysmoke.png){width="65%"}

1.  How can we assess how strong is the evidence that there is a
    difference? Conduct an appropriate analysis.

    **Solution:**

      ------------- --------------------------------- --------------------------------- -----------------------------------
                                           Non-smoker                            Smoker                          Difference
      Sample size                                 873                               126 
      Sample mean                                7.14                              6.83                                0.31
      Sample SD                                  1.52                              1.39 
      SE              $\frac{1.52}{\sqrt{873}}=0.051$   $\frac{1.39}{\sqrt{126}}=0.123$   $\sqrt{0.051^2 + 0.123^2}= 0.134$
      ------------- --------------------------------- --------------------------------- -----------------------------------

    $$t = \frac{\text{observed} - \text{hypothesized}}{\text{SE}} = \frac{0.31 - 0}{0.134} = 2.36$$
    With a p-value of 0.02 we have some/moderate evidence to reject the
    null hypothesis and conclude that the population mean birthweight of
    babies whose mothers are smokers is less than the population mean
    birthweight of babies whose mothers are nonsmokers. There is some,
    but not strong, evidence, that birthweight tends to be less on
    average for babies of mothers who are smokers than for babies who
    mothers are nonsmokers.

2.  How can we assess the size of the difference? Conduct an appropriate
    analysis.

    **Solution:** 95% CI
    $$\text{observed statistic} \pm \text{multiple} \times \text{SE:} \qquad 0.31 \pm 2 \times 0.123 \Longrightarrow \qquad [0.05, 0.58]$$
    We estimate with 95% confidence that that the population mean
    birthweight of babies whose mothers are smokers is between 0.05 and
    0.58 pounds less than the population mean birthweight of babies
    whose mothers are nonsmokers.

-   **Two-sample $t$ test for a difference in population (or treatment)
    means.**

-   Situation: binary explanatory variable (population/treatment 1, 2)
    and numerical response variable

-   Parameter: $\mu_1-\mu_2$ is the difference in population means
    (treatment means)

-   Goal: assess the strength of the evidence against the "no
    difference" or "no treatment effect" hypothesis

-   The null hypothesis is $H_0: \mu_1-\mu_2=0$

-   The alternative hypothesis is one of $H_a: \mu_1-\mu_2>0$,
    $H_a: \mu_1-\mu_2<0$, or $H_a: \mu_1-\mu_2\neq0$

-   Statistic: $\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2$ is the difference in sample means
    for samples (groups) of size $n_1, n_2$

-   The SE of the difference in sample means is
    $$\textrm{SE}(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} = \sqrt{\textrm{SE}^2(\bar{x}_1)+\textrm{SE}^2(\bar{x}_2)}$$

-   Test statistic:
    $$t = \frac{\text{observed}-\text{hypothesized}}{\text{SE}} = \frac{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2-0}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}$$

-   The p-value is the probability of observing a value at least as
    extreme as $t$, in the tail direction indicated by the alternative
    hypothesis, for the $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
    (When in doubt, use a two-sided alternative and a two-tailed
    p-value.)

-   Assumptions:

    -   Either

        -   The data are obtained through two unbiased and independent
            random samples from large populations

            -   Or from one unbiased random sample which is classified
                according to two variables, and the two groups can be
                considered independent of each other.

        -   The data are obtained from an experiment in which subjects
            were to two treatments.

    -   No bias in data collection

    -   Difference in population means is the parameter you want to
        estimate

-   The $t$ procedures for population means are valid as long as the
    sample size is large enough, regardless of the shape of the
    population distribution.

-   **However, if the population distributions are highly skewed, then
    the population *medians* might be more appropriate parameters to
    consider as measures of center.**

-   Which is more appropriate, the population means or the population
    medians, depends on the purpose for the inference.

-   Also remember that sample means and SDs, and hence $t$ procedures,
    are sensitive to outliers and extreme values.

-   ALWAYS PLOT YOUR DATA\
    \

::: exer
**Exercise 4**. Continuing the previous exercise.
:::

1.  The observed difference in sample means is 0.31 pounds. Does that
    seem like a large or meaningful difference?

    **Solution:** Birthweights vary naturally from baby to baby by about
    1.5 pounds (sample SD), so 0.3 pounds doesn't seem large relative to
    the natural variability in birthweights.\

2.  Would an observed difference of 1 pound seem like a large or
    meaningful difference?

    **Solution:** This is certainly a larger difference than 0.3 pounds.
    A difference of 0.3 pounds is only about 0.2 SDs (0.3/1.5) but a
    difference of 1 pound is 0.67 SDs (1/1.5).\

3.  Suppose this had been a study comparing weights of adult smokers
    versus non-smokers. Would an observed difference of 1 pound be a
    large or meaningful difference?

    **Solution:** There is a lot more variability in weights of adults
    than in weights of babies. So a 1 pound difference looks much
    smaller relative to the natural variability in weights of adults
    than it does relative to the natural variability in weights of
    babies.\

    -   **Effect size** measures the magnitude of the difference between
        groups

    -   A confidence interval can be used to measure the absolute size
        of the difference in the measurement units of the variable. But
        effect size can also be measured as a relative difference.

    -   The parameter $\mu_1-\mu_2$ measures the *absolute* difference
        between the two population means in the measurement units of the
        numerical response variable

    -   The population **effect size** measures the magnitude of the
        difference between group means *relative* to the population SD
        $$\frac{|\mu_1 - \mu_2|}{\sigma}$$

        -   The values of any quantitative variable vary naturally from
            unit to unit.

        -   The SD measures the degree to which individual values of the
            variable vary naturally, so the SD provides a natural
            "scale" for the variable

        -   The effect size compares the magnitude of the difference in
            means relative to the natural scale (SD) for the variable

    -   The population effect size can be estimated with **Cohen's $d$
        statistic** $$d = \frac{|\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2|}{s}$$

        -   $s$ is some estimate of $\sigma$, like the larger of the two
            sample SDs $s_1$ and $s_2$ (or the pooled sample SD)

    -   Rough guidelines for interpreting $d$:\
        \

          ------------- ------- -------- ------- ------------ ------
                    $d$     0.2      0.5     0.8          1.2    2.0
            Effect size   Small   Medium   Large   Very Large   Huge
                                                              
          ------------- ------- -------- ------- ------------ ------

    -   For example, when the effect size is 1.0 the median of the
        distribution with the higher mean is the 84th percentile of the
        distribution with the lower mean (assuming population
        distributions are Normal and the two population standard
        deviations are equal)\

    ![image](C:/Users/kjross/Documents/Handout_graphs/effect_size_plots){width="50%"}

    ::: center
      ------------------------------------ ------- -------- ------- ------ ------------ ------
      $d$                                    0.2     0.5      0.8    1.0       1.2       2.0
      Effect size                           Small   Medium   Large          Very Large   Huge
      Median of population 1 is                                                         
      (blank) percentile of population 2    58th     69th    79th    84th      89th      98th
                                                                                        
      ------------------------------------ ------- -------- ------- ------ ------------ ------
    :::

4.  Compute and interpret the effect size.

    **Solution:** The two sample SDs are 1.52 and 1.39; just pick the
    larger one.
    $$\text{Effect size} = \frac{\text{Observed difference in means}}{\text{sample SD}} = \frac{0.31}{1.52} = 0.2$$
    The observed mean birthweight for babies of nonsmokers is 0.2
    *standard deviations* above the observed mean birthweight for babies
    of smokers. This is a relatively small effect size.\

5.  Describe in detail how you would use bootstrapping to find a
    confidence interval for the *population effect size*. Then find and
    interpret the confidence interval.

    **Solution:** Similar to the previous part but the statistic is the
    sample effect size (Cohen's $d$ statistic). We estimate with 95%
    confidence that the population mean birthweight is between 0.04 to
    0.39 *SDs* larger for babies of non-smokers than for babies of
    smokers.

[^1]: Source:
    <http://a.espncdn.com/pdf/2015/0506/PatriotsWellsReport.pdf>
